quests.hint: Listen for the feeling described after work.
quests.explanation: 'Tired' means lacking energy; 'happy' describes a positive emotional state. Both are common adjectives for feelings. In English, 'I feel + adjective' is the standard structure for expressing how you feel.
quests.textToSpeak: I feel tired after a long day at work.
quests.correctAnswer: I feel happy after a long day at work.

quests.hint: Focus on how she feels about the exam.
quests.explanation: 'Nervous' means anxious or worried; 'excited' means enthusiastically looking forward to something. Both describe feelings about upcoming events. These emotion adjectives are essential for everyday conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: She is nervous about the important exam.
quests.correctAnswer: She is excited about the important exam.

quests.hint: Notice what the children are doing at home.
quests.explanation: 'Bored' means feeling uninterested with nothing to do; 'tired' means needing rest. Someone can be bored without being tired, or tired without being bored. These nuances matter in English conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: The children are bored watching television.
quests.correctAnswer: The children are tired watching television.

quests.hint: Pay attention to what time the meeting starts.
quests.explanation: 'Two o'clock' and 'three o'clock' sound similar but differ in the hour word. Time expressions are among the most common in spoken English - missing a number can cause serious misunderstandings.
quests.textToSpeak: The meeting starts at two o'clock sharp.
quests.correctAnswer: The meeting starts at three o'clock sharp.

quests.hint: Listen for which day of the week is mentioned.
quests.explanation: 'Friday' and 'Thursday' are consecutive weekdays. In fast English speech, 'Thursday' (THURZ-day) and 'Tuesday' can sometimes be confused. Always listen carefully for day names.
quests.textToSpeak: We always finish work on Friday afternoon.
quests.correctAnswer: We always finish work on Thursday afternoon.

quests.hint: Focus on which month school starts.
quests.explanation: 'September' and 'October' are both autumn months. In many English-speaking countries, the school year begins in September. Month names are essential vocabulary for planning and scheduling.
quests.textToSpeak: School starts again in September this year.
quests.correctAnswer: School starts again in October this year.

quests.hint: Listen carefully for how many children she has.
quests.explanation: 'Three' and 'four' are both small numbers. In English, numbers in spoken sentences carry the most important factual information - always listen for them first.
quests.textToSpeak: She has three children, all at school.
quests.correctAnswer: She has four children, all at school.

quests.hint: Pay attention to how many students are in the class.
quests.explanation: 'Twelve' and 'twenty' can sound surprisingly similar in fast speech. A common mistake is confusing '-teen' and '-ty' endings. Practice hearing 'twelve' (12) versus 'twenty' (20) carefully.
quests.textToSpeak: There are twelve students in our class.
quests.correctAnswer: There are twenty students in our class.

quests.hint: Focus on how many hours he spent on homework.
quests.explanation: 'Two hours' and 'three hours' differ by just one hour - but that changes the sentence significantly. In English, 'spend + time + on + activity' is a very common structure.
quests.textToSpeak: He spent two hours on his homework last night.
quests.correctAnswer: He spent three hours on his homework last night.

quests.hint: Listen for when the bird sings.
quests.explanation: 'Morning' and 'evening' are opposite times of day. 'In the morning' means before noon; 'in the evening' means after sunset. Time expressions like these give essential context to sentences.
quests.textToSpeak: The bird sings beautifully in the morning.
quests.correctAnswer: The bird sings beautifully in the evening.

quests.hint: Notice the colour of the dog.
quests.explanation: 'Brown' and 'black' are both dark colours used to describe animals. When describing pets or animals, colour adjectives come before the noun: 'a brown dog', 'a black cat'. Notice this word order.
quests.textToSpeak: She has a friendly brown dog at home.
quests.correctAnswer: She has a friendly black dog at home.

quests.hint: Pay attention to where the fish live.
quests.explanation: 'River' is freshwater flowing through land; 'sea' is a large saltwater body. Fish can live in either, but different species prefer different environments. 'Live in the...' is the correct phrase for where animals live.
quests.textToSpeak: The fish live in the fast-flowing river.
quests.correctAnswer: The fish live in the calm blue sea.

quests.hint: Listen for which type of pain he has.
quests.explanation: A 'headache' is pain in your head; a 'toothache' is pain in your tooth. Both compound nouns follow the pattern '[body part] + ache'. This is a productive word-formation pattern in English.
quests.textToSpeak: He has a very bad headache this morning.
quests.correctAnswer: He has a very bad toothache this morning.

quests.hint: Focus on what the doctor told her to do more of.
quests.explanation: 'Water' and 'vegetables' are both healthy things to consume. The doctor's advice 'drink more water' and 'eat more vegetables' are classic English health recommendations you'll hear very often.
quests.textToSpeak: The doctor told her to drink more water.
quests.correctAnswer: The doctor told her to eat more vegetables.

quests.hint: Notice when she exercises.
quests.explanation: 'Every morning before breakfast' and 'every evening after dinner' are both time expressions for daily routines. The difference between 'before' and 'after' completely changes the meaning.
quests.textToSpeak: She exercises every morning before breakfast.
quests.correctAnswer: She exercises every evening after dinner.

quests.hint: Listen for the colour of his shirt.
quests.explanation: 'Blue' and 'white' are both common colours for work shirts. In English, the adjective always comes before the noun in a noun phrase: 'a blue shirt', not 'a shirt blue'. This word order is fixed.
quests.textToSpeak: He wears a blue shirt to the office.
quests.correctAnswer: He wears a white shirt to the office.

quests.hint: Pay attention to the frequency adverb.
quests.explanation: 'Always' means 100% of the time; 'rarely' means almost never. These frequency adverbs appear between the subject and the main verb: 'She always wears...' or 'She rarely wears...'
quests.textToSpeak: She always wears glasses when she reads.
quests.correctAnswer: She rarely wears glasses when she reads.

quests.hint: Focus on which uniform the students wear.
quests.explanation: 'School uniform' is the standard clothing for academic classes; 'sports uniform' is worn for PE or sport. Both are types of uniforms - 'uniform' is a useful word meaning standardised clothing.
quests.textToSpeak: The students wear their school uniform every day.
quests.correctAnswer: The students wear their sports uniform every day.

quests.hint: Listen for which medical profession is mentioned.
quests.explanation: A 'doctor' is a general medical professional; a 'dentist' is a specialist for teeth. Both work in healthcare. When discussing jobs in English, 'My father is a...' followed by the job title is a very common structure.
quests.textToSpeak: My father has been a doctor for twenty years.
quests.correctAnswer: My father has been a dentist for twenty years.

quests.hint: Notice which school subject she teaches.
quests.explanation: 'Science' covers biology, chemistry, and physics; 'history' covers past events and civilisations. Both are important school subjects. When describing jobs, 'She teaches + subject' is the standard English structure.
quests.textToSpeak: She teaches science at the local secondary school.
quests.correctAnswer: She teaches history at the local secondary school.

quests.hint: Pay attention to his job title.
quests.explanation: A 'driver' operates vehicles; a 'manager' oversees a team or business. Both are common job titles in English. Notice that job titles follow 'works as a...' - this is the standard English phrasing.
quests.textToSpeak: He works as a driver for a delivery company.
quests.correctAnswer: He works as a manager for a delivery company.

quests.hint: Listen for which piece of furniture is in the living room.
quests.explanation: A 'sofa' is a long seat for two or more people; an 'armchair' is a comfortable chair with arm supports for one person. Both are living room furniture. 'There is a...' is used for describing single items.
quests.textToSpeak: There is a comfortable sofa in the living room.
quests.correctAnswer: There is a comfortable armchair in the living room.

quests.hint: Focus on which appliance they bought.
quests.explanation: A 'washing machine' cleans clothes; a 'dishwasher' cleans dishes. Both are common household appliances. 'We just bought a new...' is a great phrase for talking about recent purchases.
quests.textToSpeak: We just bought a new washing machine.
quests.correctAnswer: We just bought a new dishwasher.

quests.hint: Pay attention to the colour she painted the walls.
quests.explanation: 'Yellow' and 'white' are both common wall colours. Describing home decoration is a very useful everyday topic. 'She painted the walls + colour' is the natural English word order for this type of sentence.
quests.textToSpeak: She painted the walls of her bedroom yellow.
quests.correctAnswer: She painted the walls of her bedroom white.

quests.hint: Listen for which city she is visiting.
quests.explanation: 'London' is the capital of the UK; 'Paris' is the capital of France. Both are famous European cities often mentioned in travel conversations. City names appear frequently in speaking about plans and trips.
quests.textToSpeak: She is planning a trip to London in July.
quests.correctAnswer: She is planning a trip to Paris in July.

quests.hint: Notice which country he has never visited.
quests.explanation: 'Japan' and 'China' are both large East Asian countries. Both names end in a similar sound, so listen carefully. 'He has never been to...' is a useful structure using the present perfect for life experiences.
quests.textToSpeak: He has never been to Japan before.
quests.correctAnswer: He has never been to China before.

quests.hint: Focus on which country they are visiting.
quests.explanation: 'Spain' and 'Italy' are both popular European holiday destinations. Both are two-syllable country names. 'Going on holiday to...' is the British English phrase; Americans say 'going on vacation to...'
quests.textToSpeak: They are going on holiday to Spain this summer.
quests.correctAnswer: They are going on holiday to Italy this summer.

quests.hint: Listen for the name used in the greeting.
quests.explanation: 'John' and 'James' are both common English male first names. When greeting someone by name, English speakers often say 'It's lovely to see you, [Name]' - using the name at the end adds warmth.
quests.textToSpeak: It is lovely to see you again, John.
quests.correctAnswer: It is lovely to see you again, James.

quests.hint: Notice the adjective describing how the speaker feels.
quests.explanation: 'Happy' and 'glad' are near-synonyms both meaning pleased or delighted. 'Glad' is slightly more formal. In English, small differences between near-synonyms affect tone and register - an important skill for fluent speakers.
quests.textToSpeak: I am very happy to be here with you.
quests.correctAnswer: I am very glad to be here with you.

quests.hint: Pay attention to the final noun in the sentence.
quests.explanation: 'Help' and 'support' are near-synonyms but with different nuances. 'Help' is more practical and immediate; 'support' can be emotional, practical, or long-term. 'Thank you for your...' is a key polite phrase.
quests.textToSpeak: Thank you so much for all your help.
quests.correctAnswer: Thank you so much for all your support.
